title: How Ranveer Singh Destroyed the Nepo Kids' Empire in Bollywood
description:
In this video, we discuss how Bollywood has long operated through a lobby and nepotism-driven system. Star kids often continue getting big projects even after delivering multiple flops and causing huge losses to producers, while talented outsiders struggle for opportunities and recognition.

We also look at the recent controversy involving Ranveer Singh. When FWICE reportedly took action against him, many people questioned why similar action was never taken against established insiders despite past controversies involving several big Bollywood stars.

We then explore how the industry is slowly changing. FWICE eventually had to soften its stance, and even major production houses like Dharma Productions have undergone significant changes in ownership and influence. These developments suggest that the traditional power structures in Bollywood may be weakening, making it harder for nepotism alone to guarantee success in today's industry.

comments.text:
Bro

Nepotism, in the strict sense, usually refers to people in positions of public trust—politicians or bureaucrats—using public power or public resources to unfairly benefit their relatives.

Bollywood is different. A producer is investing their own private money, not taxpayer money. If a producer wants to launch their son, daughter, friend, or even a complete outsider, that’s entirely their choice. They take the financial risk, and if the film fails, they absorb the loss.

More importantly, why is any producer obligated to launch new faces? They aren’t. It’s their money, their investment, and their decision. They have every right to back whoever they believe will give them the best return—or even to make a bad business decision if they want. Their money, their choice


Also, if you’re going to use “nepotism” as the yardstick, then apply it consistently. Ranveer Singh also comes from a film-connected family and is related to the Kapoor family, so selectively labeling some actors while ignoring others only weakens the argument.

It feels like the topic gets revived only when it suits a particular narrative or when a specific film becomes the target. Either have a consistent standard for everyone, or stop milking the issue whenever it’s convenient.
